sources.title: Water

sources.title: Food

Do not eat from cans that are swollen, dented or corroded.

The page does not tell the reader to switch an ioniser off.
sources.note: Added and opened during the accuracy pass.

sources.title: Understanding Deposit Insurance
key_facts: Deposits are insured to at least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category.
Only deposits at FDIC-insured banks are covered; stocks, bonds, funds, annuities, crypto and safe-deposit box contents are not.
BankFind checks whether a bank is insured; EDIE estimates your coverage.

sources.title: Share Insurance Coverage
key_facts: Accounts at federally insured credit unions are insured to $250,000; joint and IRA accounts get separate coverage.
Some state-chartered credit unions use private insurance not backed by the US government.
The Credit Union Locator confirms federal insurance; a Share Insurance Estimator is on MyCreditUnion.gov.

sources.title: What happens if I have a joint bank account with someone who died?
key_facts: With rights of survivorship, the money passes to the surviving owner or owners.
Held as tenants in common, the deceased owner's share goes to their heirs under their will or state law.
Check the account agreement or ask the bank or credit union how the account is set up.

sources.title: Your Insured Deposits
key_facts: For payable-on-death (informal revocable trust) accounts, beneficiaries must be named in the bank's deposit records.
After an owner dies, the FDIC insures the accounts as if the owner were alive for six months.
No grace period applies when a payable-on-death beneficiary dies.

sources.title: Planning for diminished capacity and illness
key_facts: Add a trusted contact to brokerage accounts; banks and credit unions may offer emergency contacts.
Trusted contacts do not get access to your money or the power to make decisions.
Store records safely and tell trusted people where they are; keep contact and authority details up to date.
Social Security Advance Designation lets you name up to three possible representative payees.
A financial power of attorney gives someone the legal authority to make financial decisions for you if you cannot, and a durable one stays in effect if you become incapacitated.
Trusted contacts do not have access to your money.
Suggests talking to your bank, credit union or financial professional about emergency contacts and keeping them informed of who has authority over the account.
Trusted contacts do not have access to your money; the institution may contact them if it sees signs of financial exploitation.
An emergency contact generally does not let the person make investment or financial decisions for you.
A financial power of attorney gives someone the legal authority to make financial decisions for you if you cannot.
Give copies of key documents to trusted loved ones or tell them where to find them.

sources.title: What You Should Know About Your Retirement Plan
key_facts: In most 401(k) and similar plans, the balance generally goes to the surviving spouse; naming someone else needs the spouse's witnessed consent.
If you have no spouse you should name a beneficiary.
Tell your employer or plan administrator about any change in marital status and complete the forms to update it.
Check benefit statements for accuracy, including the beneficiary designation and marital status.

sources.title: Life insurance guide
key_facts: The beneficiary is the person named in the policy to receive the death benefit; you can name more than one.
Group life through an employer is usually term cover, often one or two times salary, and typically ends when you leave the job.
Life cover generally matters for people with others who depend on them financially.

sources.title: What's disability insurance and how does it work?
key_facts: Disability insurance replaces part of your income if illness or disability stops you working.
Ask first whether your job provides it; if not, you can buy a policy yourself.
Short-term policies usually pay up to a year; long-term policies pay for the years stated in the policy.

sources.title: Umbrella policy: What is it and when do you need one?
key_facts: An umbrella policy pays after home or auto liability cover runs out and covers everyone in the household.
Cover typically starts around $300,000 and reaches at least $1 million.
Ask your agent or insurer for a quote.

sources.title: Shopping Tips and Information (Homeowners and Renters)
key_facts: Insure your home for at least 80 percent of its replacement value.
Check with your agent at least once a year that cover is adequate; remodelling can raise rebuilding cost.
Make a home inventory with photos or video, receipts and serial numbers, and store copies safely.

sources.title: Homeowners and Renters Definitions
key_facts: Additional living expenses pays costs above normal living costs while the home is repaired after an insured loss.
Replacement cost pays without depreciation; actual cash value subtracts depreciation.
Typical exclusions include earthquake, sewer backup or sump pump failure, ordinance or law, and intentional loss; sewer backup cover can be added.
An umbrella policy sits above other cover and needs a set amount of underlying liability cover.

sources.title: Disasters
key_facts: Before a disaster, review your policies and know the difference between actual cash value and replacement cost.
Ask whether your policy pays additional living expenses.
Basic homeowners policies do not cover flood, earthquake or mine subsidence; cover can be added.
Keep copies of policies and your inventory away from home.

sources.title: Flood Insurance
key_facts: Flood cover is not usually part of homeowners or renters policies and is bought separately.
Flood insurance usually takes effect 30 days after purchase.

sources.title: Auto Insurance Definitions
key_facts: Comprehensive cover pays for non-collision damage or loss such as hail, vandalism, flood, fire and theft.
Collision cover pays for hitting another vehicle or object, or overturning.
Rental reimbursement is an optional benefit that pays for a rental car during repairs.

sources.title: Does my homeowners insurance policy cover flooding?
key_facts: Flood damage is not typically covered by a homeowners insurance policy.

sources.title: Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts
key_facts: A credit freeze is free to place and lift and does not affect your credit score.
You must contact each of Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
Parents can request a free freeze for a child under 16, which stays until removed.
An initial fraud alert lasts one year; an extended alert lasts seven years.
A parent can request a free credit freeze for a child under 16; it stays until the bureaus are told to remove it.
The page says nothing about 16- and 17-year-olds.

sources.title: Free Credit Reports
key_facts: AnnualCreditReport.com is the only authorised site for free reports; you can also order by phone.
Each nationwide bureau gives a free report at least every 12 months, and the bureaus have made weekly free reports permanent.
Beware imposter sites and unsolicited messages asking for your Social Security number.

sources.title: State consumer protection offices
key_facts: Lists each state's consumer protection office, which can help with complaints against businesses and investigate scams and fraud.

sources.title: Consumer alert: storm-related repair scams (July 1, 2026)
key_facts: Warns of storm chasers and fake public adjusters after storms.
Get written estimates and contracts, do not pay in full until work is done, avoid cash and payment apps.
Report suspicious activity to local police or the Attorney General's Consumer Fraud Hotline.

sources.title: How long should I keep records?
key_facts: Generally keep records until the period of limitations ends, usually 3 years; 6 years for substantially underreported income; 7 years for bad-debt or worthless-securities claims.
Keep property records until the limitations period ends for the year you dispose of the property.
Keep copies of filed returns; check whether insurers or lenders need records kept longer.

sources.title: Preparing for a disaster (taxpayers and businesses)
key_facts: Scan tax records such as W-2s and returns, back them up and store backups away from home.
Use Publication 584 to list belongings room by room and photograph or film home contents.
Form 4506 gets copies of past returns; free transcripts cover the current and three prior years.

sources.title: Get an identity protection PIN
key_facts: A six-digit IP PIN stops others filing a tax return with your SSN or ITIN.
Anyone who can verify identity can get one; parents can request one for dependants.
A new PIN is issued every calendar year; online enrollees must retrieve it each year.
The page says the online IP PIN system is offline from November 16, 2026 to mid-January 2027.

sources.title: Online account for individuals
key_facts: View balances, payments, transcripts and IRS digital notices.
Make and schedule payments and manage payment plans.
Get an IP PIN and approve authorisations from a tax professional.

sources.title: Tax relief in disaster situations
key_facts: Lists IRS disaster relief by date and state, with postponed deadlines based on FEMA declarations.
Points to DisasterAssistance.gov for non-tax help.

sources.title: Reconstructing records after a natural disaster or casualty loss
key_facts: Free transcripts through Get Transcript online, by phone, or Form 4506-T; copies of past returns with Form 4506.
Writing the disaster designation on Form 4506 or 4506-T speeds processing and waives the fee.
Publication 584 is the casualty, disaster and theft loss workbook for personal property.

sources.title: Advance Directives
key_facts: Illinois recognises a health-care power of attorney, a living will, a mental health treatment preference declaration and a POLST form, and the page links IDPH forms for each.
Health-care power of attorney: the agent may not be your health-care provider; a person who is not the agent should witness; an electronic copy may be shown if the original is not available.
Living will applies only to a terminal condition, needs two witnesses, and your health-care professional may not be one.

Mental health declaration needs two witnesses (not your health-care professional, an employee of your facility or a relative); any attorney-in-fact must accept in writing; it expires three years after signing.
Tell your health-care professionals about any directive and give copies to them and to the people you appoint; directives can be cancelled.
Health-care power of attorney: the agent cannot be your health-care professional or other health-care provider; someone who is not your agent should witness your signing.
Living will: two people must witness your signing; your health-care professional cannot be a witness; you must tell your health-care professional that you have one.
The Uniform POLST order needs your signature or that of your authorised legal representative, and the signature of your attending practitioner.

sources.title: Legal Forms - Advance Directives
key_facts: Links the Power of Attorney for Property form hosted by the Department on Aging and the IDPH health-care, living will, mental health and POLST forms.
Says the forms may be used by the public and come in English and Spanish.

sources.title: Illinois Statutory Short Form Power of Attorney for Property (form, based on 755 ILCS 45/3-3 eff. July 27, 2015)
key_facts: Form states the power is not effective unless signed by at least one witness and notarised, and the notary may not also be the witness.
Witness may not be the agent or successor agent, the attending physician or mental health provider or their relative, or a relative of the principal or agent.
Successor agents may be named, but not co-agents; the agent's powers can continue after the principal becomes incapacitated.
The power is not effective unless signed by at least one witness and the principal's signature is notarised; the notary may not also sign as a witness.

The witness certifies they are not the attending physician or mental health service provider or a relative of one; not an owner or operator (or relative of one) of a health-care facility where the principal is a patient or resident; not a parent, sibling or descendant, or the spouse of one, of the principal or of any agent or successor agent; and not an agent or successor agent.
The form itself prints these limits for the witness only; it does not print them for the notary.

sources.title: 755 ILCS 5/11-5.4 Short-term guardian
key_facts: A parent may appoint a short-term guardian of a minor in writing without court approval.
The instrument must be dated and signed before at least two witnesses aged 18 or over, neither of them the short-term guardian, and the short-term guardian also signs.
If another parent is willing and able to care for the child, that parent must consent by signing.
Authority lasts 365 days from the effective date unless the instrument sets a different end; only one appointment may be in force at a time.
Signed by, or at the direction of, the appointing parent in the presence of at least 2 credible witnesses at least 18 years of age, neither of whom is the person appointed as the short-term guardian.
The person appointed as the short-term guardian shall also sign the written instrument, but need not sign at the same time.
Effective for a period of 365 days from the date the appointment is effective, unless the written instrument provides for the appointment to terminate upon a different specified date or event.
Subsections (d-5) and (e-10) cover renewal after an administrative separation and a parent on active military duty.

sources.title: 755 ILCS 5/11-5.3 Appointment of standby guardian
key_facts: A parent may designate a standby guardian of a minor in any writing, including a will, witnessed by two adults who are not the standby guardian.
A standby guardian is appointed by a court on petition; the designation does not affect the other parent's rights.

sources.title: 755 ILCS 27/40 Real Property Transfer on Death Instrument Act: requirements
key_facts: A transfer on death instrument must have the formalities of a recordable deed, state that the transfer happens at the owner's death, and be recorded with the county recorder before the owner's death.
Failing any requirement makes the instrument void.

sources.title: 755 ILCS 27/45 Signing, attestation, and acknowledgment
key_facts: The owner signs, two or more credible witnesses attest, and the signatures are acknowledged before a notary.
Without at least two credible witnesses the instrument is void; a beneficiary who witnesses risks losing their share.

sources.title: 755 ILCS 65/10 Disposition of Remains Act: form
key_facts: Sets out the 'Appointment of Agent to Control Disposition of Remains' form, with successor agents, special directions and cremation choices, and a notary block.

sources.title: 755 ILCS 65/5 Right to control disposition; priority
key_facts: A person named in a written instrument meeting Sections 10 and 15 comes first in the right to control disposition of remains, ahead of the executor, spouse and adult children.

sources.title: Your Guide to Estate Planning
key_facts: An Illinois will needs a maker aged 18 or over of sound mind and two witnesses; beneficiaries should not witness; a will can name a guardian for minor children and the executor.
Powers of attorney for property and for health care end at death and do not replace a will; a living will and a health-care power should agree.
Illinois allows certain real estate to pass at death by a transfer on death instrument.
Joint tenancy, tenancy in common and tenancy by the entirety pass property differently; joint tenancy is not a substitute for a will.
A will generally does not control property with a named beneficiary; life changes and changes in the law can call for an update.
Guide dated 2021; points to the ISBA lawyer finder.
The maker of an Illinois will must be 18 and of sound mind and memory; the will must be in writing.
The will must be signed by the maker and witnessed by two witnesses in the special manner provided by law.
People who are beneficiaries under the will cannot serve as witnesses.
The guide does not say the witnesses must all be present together, and does not mention digital assets.

sources.title: MCL 700.2519 Michigan statutory will
key_facts: A will following the statutory form is valid; the form is printed in the statute.
Requires signature and at least two adult witnesses (three preferred) who sign a statement.
The form lets the maker nominate a guardian for children under 18 and a conservator, with alternates.

sources.title: MCL 700.2515 Deposit of will with court in testator's lifetime
key_facts: A will in a sealed wrapper may be deposited with the probate court of the county where the testator lives; the court keeps it and issues a certificate of deposit for a fee.
During the testator's life it is released only to the testator or a person authorised in writing.

sources.title: MCL 700.5103 Delegation of parental or guardian powers
key_facts: A parent may delegate powers over a minor's care, custody or property by a properly executed power of attorney for up to 180 days (longer for a deployed service member).
Consent to adoption cannot be delegated.
A parent or guardian may delegate powers over a minor by a properly executed power of attorney for a period not exceeding 180 days.
If the parent is serving in the armed forces and deployed to a foreign nation, and the power of attorney says so, the delegation lasts until the thirty-first day after the deployment ends.
The power to consent to adoption cannot be delegated.
Reopened for LG-26: a parent or guardian may delegate powers by a properly executed power of attorney for up to 180 days (deployed service member: until the 31st day after deployment ends).
The section says nothing about the other parent signing, consenting or being notified.

sources.title: MCL 700.5202 Parental appointment of guardian for minor
key_facts: A parent may appoint a guardian for an unmarried minor by will or by another signed writing attested by at least two witnesses.
The appointment takes effect when the guardian's acceptance is filed with the court.

sources.title: MCL 556.205 Uniform Power of Attorney Act: execution
key_facts: A power of attorney must be signed by the principal and, to be durable, acknowledged before a notary or signed before two witnesses who also sign.
A nominated agent may not be a witness; the act took effect July 1, 2024 for powers made on or after that date.
A power of attorney is signed by the principal, or in the principal's conscious presence by another individual the principal directs to sign.
A power the principal signs is durable if it is acknowledged before a notary (or other officer who takes acknowledgments) or signed in the presence of two witnesses who also sign.
A witness may not be an agent nominated in the power.
A power signed by another person at the principal's direction is durable only if signed before two witnesses, whether or not it is also acknowledged.

sources.title: MCL 556.401 Statutory form power of attorney
key_facts: Sets out a statutory form power of attorney with agent and successor agents, general and specific authority, signature, witness and notary blocks, and the agent's duties.

sources.title: MCL 700.5506 Designation of patient advocate
key_facts: An adult of sound mind may designate a patient advocate for care, custody and medical or mental health treatment decisions.
The designation must be written, signed, dated and witnessed by two people who are not close relatives, heirs, the physician, the advocate or certain insurer and facility employees.
It must be placed in the patient's medical record before it takes effect.

sources.title: Probate Information: Patient Advocate Designation
key_facts: You and two witnesses must sign; witness restrictions are listed.
The patient advocate can act only after signing an acceptance and after two professionals find you unable to decide.
Without a designation a probate court may be asked to appoint a guardian.

sources.title: MCL 700.3206 Funeral arrangements; funeral representative
key_facts: An adult of sound mind may designate a funeral representative in a written, dated, signed designation, which may be part of a will or patient advocate designation.
It must be signed before two witnesses who are not the representative, or acknowledged before a notary.
Without a designation, decisions fall to the spouse, then adult children and other relatives in a set order.

sources.title: MCL 700.2807 Revocation by divorce or annulment
key_facts: Divorce or annulment revokes gifts and fiduciary nominations to a former spouse in a will or other governing instrument unless the document or a court order says otherwise.

sources.title: MCL 700.1004 Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act: user direction
key_facts: A user may direct disclosure of digital assets through a custodian's online tool, or in a will, trust or power of attorney.
A direction made in a qualifying online tool overrides a contrary direction in a will, trust or power of attorney.

sources.title: MCL 257.236 Transfer of vehicle on death of owner
key_facts: A surviving spouse or heir may have a dead owner's vehicle retitled through the Secretary of State with proof of death, if the vehicles' value is under a set limit and no other estate property needs probate.

Reopened for LG-10: if an owner of vehicles dies leaving no other property needing letters of authority, the surviving spouse or an heir may get title from the Secretary of State when the vehicles' total value is under the statutory cap ($100,000 for 2024 and 2025, adjusted yearly from 2026).

sources.title: Managing someone else's money
key_facts: Guides for people named in a power of attorney to make decisions about money and property, for trustees and for court-appointed guardians.
Encourages planning ahead in case you need help managing money in future.

sources.title: Advance Directives
key_facts: Advance directives are legal documents recording care decisions in advance.
A living will states which treatments you would want; a health-care power of attorney names a proxy to decide if you cannot.

sources.title: Five Things to Know About Safe Deposit Boxes, Home Safes and Your Valuables
key_facts: A box suits original documents such as deeds and titles, but not items needed quickly or when the bank is closed, such as passports or powers of attorney; ask about state law for where to keep an original will.
Box contents are not FDIC-insured.
Joint renters can have unrestricted access; after an owner dies, access depends on state law.

sources.title: Standby Guardianship
key_facts: Standby guardianship lets a parent arrange in advance for a named person to take over care of a child under set conditions while keeping much of their own authority.
Laws differ by state.

sources.title: How to apply for disaster assistance
key_facts: Disaster Legal Services gives free legal help to people with low income in a federally declared disaster area, including new wills and powers of attorney lost in the disaster.

sources.title: I Need Legal Help
key_facts: Search by address to find an LSC-funded civil legal aid organisation for people with low income.

sources.title: Title and Registration Publications and Forms
key_facts: Lists the Beneficiary Affidavit, form VSD 773, among the title forms, with a link to the form. Opened in a browser on 15 November 2026.

sources.title: Corrected Title – Deceased
key_facts: How a vehicle title is transferred after the owner dies depends on whether the title was in the owner's name alone or in joint ownership, and, if alone, on whether the estate is being probated. Opened in a browser on 15 November 2026.

sources.title: Titles
key_facts: Under “Deceased owner”: if the title is in both the survivor's and the deceased's names with the legend “Full Rights to Survivor”, the title, a copy of the death certificate and identification are all that is needed. Separate steps are given for a vehicle that is probated, one that is not, and several next of kin. Opened in a browser on 15 November 2026.

sources.title: 225 ILCS 85/15.3 Emergency prescription refills
key_facts: A pharmacist may use professional judgment to give an emergency supply of medicine for a chronic condition when the prescriber cannot be reached for refill authorisation.

Conditions: stopping the medicine could cause harm or suffering; the same pharmacy has filled that prescription for that patient before; it is not a controlled substance; the patient is told future refills need the prescriber; the prescriber is informed.
The supply is limited to the emergency period and may not exceed 30 days.
The section is marked as scheduled for repeal on January 1, 2028 (source P.A. 100-237, effective 18 August 2017).

sources.title: MCL 333.17751 (Public Health Code, dispensing prescription drugs)
key_facts: Prescription drugs may be dispensed only under an original prescription or an approved equivalent record.
A pharmacist may dispense additional quantities only up to the total the prescriber authorised; this does not apply to most controlled substances.
The section contains no emergency-refill provision for when a prescriber cannot be reached; latest amendment listed is 2024 Act 242, effective 2 April 2025.

sources.publisher: Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (HHS)
sources.title: Emergency Prescription Assistance Program
key_facts: EPAP helps people without health insurance get prescription drugs, vaccines, medical supplies and equipment during certain declared emergencies.
It is not switched on for every federally declared disaster; the page lists current activations.
The page offers a search for EPAP-enrolled pharmacies.

sources.publisher: Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (HHS)
sources.title: Get It: Get It, Check It, Use It
key_facts: Check the provider's patient portal first; some records, such as immunisations, may already be there.
Requests can be made through the portal, a release or access form, email, mail or fax.
Providers have up to 30 days to supply records, with one extension of up to 30 days if they give a reason; state law may be shorter.
Electronic delivery is likely free; a reasonable cost-based fee may be charged for copies.

sources.publisher: Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (HHS)
sources.title: Your Health Information Rights
key_facts: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule you may see and get a copy of your health and billing records from covered providers and health plans.
Most requests must be met within 30 days (60 days if records are off-site), with one 30-day extension if explained in writing.
Searching for and retrieving records cannot be charged for; copying and mailing may be.
Where state and federal law differ, the provider follows the one giving you more rights.

sources.title: Staying Up to Date with Your Vaccine Records
key_facts: No national body keeps vaccination records.

Places to look: parents' records and baby books, school or college health services, past employers including the military, doctors and public health clinics, and the state health department's immunisation information system.
Keep your own record form, ask providers to sign and date it, and store it with your other important documents.

sources.title: Emergency Kit Checklist: Pregnant Women, Infants, and Children
key_facts: Kit for everyone includes medical, pharmacy, mental-health, family and emergency contact numbers and copies of important documents in a waterproof container.
For a pregnant person: a plan made with the provider for where to get prenatal care or deliver if the usual office or hospital is closed.
For an infant: a copy of vaccination records.

sources.title: Safety Messages for Pregnant, Postpartum, and Breastfeeding Women During Natural Disasters and Severe Weather
key_facts: Plan with the health care provider where to get prenatal care or give birth if the office or hospital is closed.
Keep medical records, insurance information, ID and prescription details in a waterproof, portable container.
Keep 7 to 10 days of prescription medicine, ask about a 30-day or longer emergency refill, and check your state's emergency prescription rules.
Tell shelter staff you are pregnant as soon as possible.

sources.title: HIPAA Basics for Providers: Privacy, Security, & Breach Notification Rules (MLN909001, May 2025)
key_facts: Unless the patient objects, providers may share information with family, friends or anyone the patient names as involved in their care.
Providers may tell a family member or anyone responsible for the patient's care about the patient's general condition or location.
Providers may share information about a patient who is incapacitated if they believe it is in the patient's best interest.

sources.title: You have rights in an emergency room under EMTALA
key_facts: Hospital emergency departments must give a medical screening exam even if you have no insurance.
You cannot be refused screening or emergency treatment because you cannot pay.
If you have an emergency condition the hospital must offer stabilising treatment or an appropriate transfer.

sources.title: Medical bill rights
key_facts: The No Surprises Act protects you from unexpected out-of-network bills for emergency room visits.
Protections also cover certain non-emergency care at in-network facilities and air ambulance services.

sources.title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
key_facts: The page directs anyone in crisis to call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

sources.title: Advance Care Planning: Advance Directives for Health Care
key_facts: An out-of-hospital DNR order tells emergency medical personnel your wishes about restarting heartbeat or breathing when you are not in hospital.

POLST or MOLST forms are medical orders professionals can act on at once in an emergency; they are usually made near the end of life or when critically ill, and may also be called POST; check with your state health department.
You may also want to document your wishes about organ and tissue donation; the page points to OrganDonor.gov.

sources.title: POLST Guidance for Individuals
key_facts: The IDPH Uniform POLST form is a voluntary medical order, completed with a practitioner, recording decisions about CPR and life-sustaining treatment.
It is suggested for people with serious or life-limiting illness and for people who do not want CPR.
No witness is required; photocopies of a valid form are generally followed.
Keep it where you live, where emergency personnel can find it quickly (the page suggests the refrigerator); legal decision makers should have a copy.
Illinois-licensed EMS must honour a valid copy; older IDPH Uniform DNR and DNR/POLST forms remain valid.
The patient or their authorised legal representative prints and signs their name in the consent section; the form is completed with the practitioner.
A witness signature is no longer required by Illinois law and was removed from the form.
Keep the form where you live, somewhere easy to find; the legal guardian, health-care agent or surrogate should have a copy they can get to easily.

sources.title: Advance Directives
key_facts: The page offers the POLST form, living will, health care power of attorney and mental health treatment declaration forms.
It describes the POLST order as the directive that says CPR is not to be used if the heart or breathing stops; no separate DNR form is listed.
Same page as idph-advance-directives: the Uniform POLST order needs the signature of the patient or their authorised legal representative and of the attending practitioner.

sources.publisher: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services
sources.title: MI-POST
key_facts: MI-POST is an optional one-page, two-sided medical order for people with serious advanced illness or frailty, covering CPR, critical care and other care.
It guides care only if the person cannot say what they want at the time.
It is signed by the patient or patient representative and their physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant.
The page links form MDHHS-5836 (English, Arabic, Spanish), the patient and family information sheet MDHHS-5837, FAQs and the administrative rules.

sources.title: MCL 333.5677 (POST form consent)
key_facts: A capable patient, or a patient advocate or guardian for one who is not, may consent to POST medical orders.
The attending health professional must explain the form and give an information form before signing.
A copy goes in the medical record and the patient or representative keeps the original.
A capable patient, or a patient advocate or guardian for one who is not, may consent to the medical orders on a POST form, with the attending health professional.
The patient or the patient representative keeps the original POST form; the attending health professional keeps a copy in the medical record.
This section does not itself set the review timetable; MCL 333.5676 does.

sources.title: MCL 333.5674 (definitions)
key_facts: A POST patient is an adult with an advanced illness, or another condition that makes death within a year foreseeable.
A POST form is not an advance health care directive.

sources.publisher: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services
sources.title: Michigan's Do-Not-Resuscitate Procedure Act
key_facts: A competent adult who has discussed it with their physician may sign a do-not-resuscitate order; the physician must also sign (not needed for people whose religion opposes medical treatment).
Forms are available from most hospices.
Keep it in a visible place at home, tell family or friends where it is, and optionally wear a DNR bracelet.
The order is valid outside health care facilities; it can be revoked at any time and no one may require it as a condition of care.

sources.title: MCL 333.1053 (Michigan Do-Not-Resuscitate Procedure Act, execution of order)
key_facts: An adult of sound mind, or their patient advocate, may execute the order on the statutory form.
It must be signed by the declarant (or advocate), the attending physician and two adult witnesses, at least one of whom is not a close relative or presumptive heir.
The declarant or advocate keeps the order, and it must be accessible in the home; an identification bracelet may be worn.
An individual aged 18 or older of sound mind, or their patient advocate, may execute a do-not-resuscitate order.
The order is dated and signed by the declarant or patient advocate (or a person signing at the declarant's direction), the attending physician and two witnesses aged 18 or older.
At least one witness must not be the declarant's spouse, parent, child, grandchild, sibling or presumptive heir.
The declarant or patient advocate keeps the order and makes it accessible within the declarant's place of residence or other setting outside a hospital.

sources.title: MCL 333.1054 (form of do-not-resuscitate order)
key_facts: Sets out the wording of the Michigan do-not-resuscitate order, with sections for the declarant, a patient advocate, parents of a minor and a guardian, and a witness attestation.

sources.title: Organ donor registry

National Battery Ingestion Hotline 800-498-8666, or Poison Help 800-222-1222.

sources.title: Childproofing Your Home for Poisons

Keep medicines in original containers with safety caps; keep purses and bags holding medicines out of a child's reach.
Never let children handle laundry detergent packets; seal the container and lock it away after each use.

sources.title: Up and Away Campaign Resources
key_facts: Keep medicines where young children cannot reach or see them, and put them away after every use, not on the counter or at a sick child's bedside, even if another dose is due in a few hours.
Relock the cap each time; turn a twist-lock cap until it clicks or will not turn further.
Ask babysitters, houseguests and visitors to keep bags, purses and coats with medicine in them up, away and out of sight.
Teach children what medicine is and that a trusted adult gives it; never call medicine candy.
About 100 young children are brought to emergency rooms each day after getting into medicines left within reach.

Store cleaning and pesticide products out of children's reach and use childproof locks on low cabinets.

FDA-approved generics work in the same way and provide the same clinical benefit and risks as the brand.
Does not address over-the-counter or store-brand medicines. Content current as of 11/01/2021.

sources.title: The Over-the-Counter Drug Facts Label
key_facts: The label lists the active ingredient: the substance in the product that causes the intended therapeutic effect, with its strength.
Many OTC medicines may have similar brand names with different active ingredients.
Does not discuss store brands. Content current as of 09/02/2026.

sources.title: Basement and Garage Fire Safety
key_facts: "Store oil, gasoline, paints, propane and varnishes in a shed away from your home."
"Flammable liquids, storage of combustibles, gas appliances and electrical tools can lead to fires."
Page last reviewed April 1, 2023. It gives no amount and says nothing about apartments.

sources.title: Family Radio Service (FRS)
key_facts: FRS is licensed by rule: an individual license is not required to operate an FRS radio, at any age, for personal or business use.
There are 22 FRS channels in the 462 MHz and 467 MHz range, all shared with GMRS, which requires an individual license.
Channels 1 to 7 and 15 to 22 are limited to 2 W; channels 8 to 14 to 0.5 W.
The usual range of an FRS device on channels 8 to 14 is less than one-half mile; longer range is possible on the other channels depending on conditions.
An FRS transmitter may not be modified and must be certified by the FCC.

sources.title: General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS)
key_facts: GMRS is a licensed radio service on channels around 462 MHz and 467 MHz, most used for short-distance two-way voice with hand-held radios, mobile radios and repeater systems.
You may apply for a GMRS license if you are 18 or older and not a representative of a foreign government.
With a license, any family member, regardless of age, can operate GMRS stations and units within the licensed system.
In 2017 the FCC increased the license term from 5 to 10 years.
The page (updated August 14, 2024) does not state the fee, and names no examination.

sources.title: Citizens Band Radio Service (CBRS)
key_facts: CB is a private, two-way, short-distance voice communications service for personal or business activities of the general public.
It is authorized 40 channels between 26.965 MHz and 27.405 MHz.
An individual license is not required to operate a CB station.

sources.title: Amateur Radio Service
key_facts: The amateur service is for qualified persons of any age who are interested in radio technique solely with a personal aim and without pecuniary interest.
The license class is determined by the skill and knowledge the licensee demonstrates in an examination given by volunteer examiners in their community.
Most new amateur operators start at the Technician Class and may advance to General or Amateur Extra.
The written examinations are built from question pools that have been made public.
